old_title: Microsoft outage live: millions still affected as disruption stretches beyond 18 hours
new_title: Microsoft 'deeply sorry' for disruption affecting millions and says it's 'not related to cyber or AI' - as it happened
old_text:
Many Microsoft 365 services are affected, for example:
Problems with Exchange Online mean users may be unable to access their mailbox using Outlook on the web
Microsoft365Education features including Assignments, Reading Progress, and Speaker Progress may be impacted.
MicrosoftCopilot365 - users may be unable to load Copilot Chat or receive responses in the web and desktop apps
The Microsoft ToDo app may not load, and users may see operation failures.
On Teams, Microsoft says:
Most of the core functionality including joining calls, meetings, group chats, and channel messages are not impacted. Scenarios that depend on Exchange Online, including Calendar related failures with scheduling, invites, viewing, and meeting edits. Creation of Live or Virtual events fail. Failures with Copilot responses for outlook, calendar, or M365 files, read history, or adding to new chats.
Navigating to App chats, adding new contacts or syncing contacts in settings fail. Standard channels are working fine but users may experience the inability to create or delete private or shared channels.
And it warns it could take up to 48 hours to restore services fully:
City of Tampa offices are open and operating on normal schedules. Walk-in services, phone lines, and emergency operations (911) remain fully operational.
However, residents and external partners may experience delays or failures when sending emails to City of Tampa accounts or receiving emails from them. Technology teams are actively monitoring the Microsoft issue and based on vendor guidance, full service restoration is anticipated within 48 hours.
The Microsoft outage may be an - unwelcome - opportunity to test how companies and public services would cope under a serious cyber attack.
Forrester's principal analyst Dario Maisto epxlains:
"The Microsoft outage, for the little we know so far, represents the perfect quasi-natural experiment for stress testing an organization's - and even an entire continent - digital sovereignty posture.
"Although this outage does not strictly pose a sovereignty question, as this seems to be more an accident than the consequence of a government's will, it does allow us to test what would happen if interruption of mailing services and AI tools like Copilot would be the direct consequence of a political act from the government.
Microsoft has now declared that service availability continues to improve - but dome users may still have problems accessing their email.
In an updated Current Status on the outage, it says:
We're continuing to see improvements in service availability, with email queues significantly reduced and approaching normal levels. Some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery as recovery continues.
Simon Azzopardi, CEO of security firmCoreView,says IT teams need to do three things following the Microsoft outage:
"Confirm that security and compliance controls such as data loss prevention, sensitivity labelling and Intune compliance policies are working as intended.
Review every emergency change made during the outage, because workarounds made under pressure tend to become permanent gaps.
And treat delayed email with extra caution: Microsoft warned that Safe Links might not be able to check URLs during the disruption, and attackers routinely use outages as cover."
Azzopardi adds:
"Our sympathy goes out to every IT team that has spent their time keeping their organisation running without email, calendars and, in many cases, their security and compliance tools."
Suggestions include "Microsoft364" (although this might be downgraded to "Microsoft 363" if the problems drag into Saturday!), "Microsoft No-Pilot", "Friday the 13th: Nightmare on One Microsoft Way", and "MicrosoftLongWeekend" (a nod to how today has been a write-off for some companies around the world).
More people who've been affected by the outage have been getting in touch with The Guardian, including students, teachers and others who work in education.
Jenny is a teacher in SEN [special educational needs] school in Norfolk, England and teaches a four day week. Ordinarily Friday is her rest day and in the morning, she says she logs in and gives access to her colleagues to teach lessons she has pre-prepared and also responds to emails.
"I realised there was a problem at 5:30am when I tried to give access to a powerpoint presentation my TA [teaching assistant] needed for a maths lesson. I had to download this, recreate it as a pdf and then upload it to the cover planning folder. It was not a quick fix."
She also had to keep in contact with my TA via WhatsApp rather than email.
It's made her rest day a lot more stressful, Jenny explains:
"I was wrestling with this issue until 9am when I gave up as school had then started."
Jenny believes we should invest in European technology firms. "I find it very worrying that we are so reliant on US technology as we are seeing this has affected so many areas of our society today."
Meanwhile Tracy, a nursing student at the UniversityofSouthWales, says the outage has disrupted her studies, "particularly as university emails are not working".
This has made it difficult for her to access important communications from lecturers, receive updates about assignments, and stay informed about placement arrangements. "As nursing students, we rely heavily on timely communication," she says, "especially when balancing academic work with clinical placements. The outage has caused uncertainty and made it harder to keep up to date".
On the bright side, this might help nursing students to prepare for similar situations in the future, she says.
"We can see how to handle not being able to access the information. We can write everything down, we can pass on notes verbally or on paper - it's back to the old-school days."
We're seeing continued recovery progress across affected regions, with broader improvements now observed in North America and sustained improvements across much of Europe.
We're also seeing encouraging recovery signals in Asia Pacific, although some users may continue to experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery as mitigation progresses across the remaining affected infrastructure.
UK house moves are being disrupted by the Microsoft outage, it appears.
DavidStrank, who runs Kent-based Stranks Removals & Storage, said that the moves of two customers had been disrupted today while the exchange of another client was also delayed. The hold up could derail their planned move date.
"We've got two crews that are waiting for keys at the moment," Strank told the Guardian.
"They are loaded and sitting outside but can't do anything. We've got a move that we're supposed to start on 23 November and he's rung to say that they can't exchange today because they can't send any emails."

Microsoft365Education features including Assignments, Reading Progress, and Speaker Progress may be impacted.
MicrosoftCopilot365 - users may be unable to load Copilot Chat or receive responses in the web and desktop apps
The Microsoft ToDo app may not load, and users may see operation failures.
On Teams, Microsoft says:
Most of the core functionality including joining calls, meetings, group chats, and channel messages are not impacted. Scenarios that depend on Exchange Online, including Calendar related failures with scheduling, invites, viewing, and meeting edits. Creation of Live or Virtual events fail. Failures with Copilot responses for outlook, calendar, or M365 files, read history, or adding to new chats.
Navigating to App chats, adding new contacts or syncing contacts in settings fail. Standard channels are working fine but users may experience the inability to create or delete private or shared channels.
The UK government say it is seeking to establish "the full picture" of Microsoft outages.
The prime minister's deputy spokeswoman said:
"We're working with departments and with Microsoft to establish the full picture, and where services are disrupted, departments have contingency arrangements in place.
"You'll obviously appreciate this is an ongoing situation, but in the meantime, people are encouraged to follow advice on the services they require for alternative ways to get in touch."
Some UK doctors have been getting in touch, reporting that their emails are now coming back online after being disrupted by the Microsoft technical problems today.
That suggests there's progress bringing Outlook back online.
Ofqual, the exam regulator for England, is the latest educational institution to be hit by the Microsoft outage. This morning it advised users that its complaints service was not functioning:
"We are currently experiencing issues with this service, related to the global Microsoft outage.
"We are currently unable to receive complaints, whistleblowing and malpractice submissions."
It said any urgent enquiries should come by telephone.
The continued disruption at Microsoft shows the importance of building some resilience into your IT setup, points out StevenWatt, Professor of Practice in Cybersecurity at the University of St Andrews:
Organisations should be able to answer some basic questions. Which of our critical processes depend on a single supplier? How long could we operate if that supplier were unavailable? What is our fallback for communicating with staff, customers and regulators? Have we tested it, or do we simply assume it exists?
A continuity plan that relies on the same platform that has just failed is not a plan. Remember manual workarounds - these don't work any more!
new_text:
Microsoft has said it is "deeply sorry" for the disruption caused by the global outage, which it said was caused by "a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents". The company added: "We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services."
Stocks fell in shaky trading on Wall Street on Friday, but the market remains on track for a winning week. Microsoft rose 0.2%, despite suffering a global outage for its web services that disrupted email accounts and other applications.
The Microsoft outage was preventing some US prison inmates from being released. The Arapahoe County Sheriff's Office in Colorado, USA, warned they could not process bond payments, as they rely on Outlook email notifications. So unless the money is handed over in person, people could not be let out.
Some US cities reported their Microsoft services are now returning after the global outage. The sheriff's office in Arapahoe County, Colorado, which previously reported the outage was affecting online bond payments, said the issue has been resolved. The police department of Greensboro, North Carolina, also saw its services restored. It joked: "While it's not the outcome we wanted, we would like to let you know that our email is working again."
The UK government has been working with Microsoft to understand the full impact of the outage on public services, the cyber minister Baroness Elizabeth Lloyd said. She said it mainly hit "back-office functions", such as email and messaging, with 999 calls and the NHS 111 line unaffected.
The UK government has been working with Microsoft to understand the full impact of the outage on public services, the cyber minister Baroness Elizabeth Lloyd said.
She said it mainly hit "back-office functions", such as email and messaging, with 999 calls and the NHS 111 line unaffected.
Lloyd added that this has been "inconvenient and disruptive."
"Throughout the day, we have seen limited reports of impact on frontline service delivery, and I encourage people to follow advice from the services they need on alternative ways to get in touch where email or web forms may be unavailable," she added.
Hospitals, GPs, police forces and property agents across the UK have been hit by the global Microsoft outage. Here's how the disruption to email and other IT facilities has affected key services.
Healthcare
The NHS experienced "serious" and "widespread" disruption across the UK on Friday as a result of the Microsoft outage, with hundreds of hospitals, GP surgeries and community health services affected, senior health sources said.
While some doctors, hospital workers and NHS night staff told the Guardian they first noticed problems accessing emails during the early hours of Friday morning, the severity of the problem became apparent to most from about 6am.
The NHS.net Connect system - which more than one million NHS staff use for emails, meetings, calendars, file access and other tasks - is powered by Microsoft. The outage meant many could not log in, perform basic duties, or send and receive patient data needed for the delivery of healthcare.
NHS sources said the outage caused disruption to a range of Microsoft 365 services relied upon by staff, including Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive and Copilot. The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency also said it was experiencing problems sending and receiving emails.
Some staff resorted to using patients' paper records after being unable to access email and other IT facilities. An NHS England spokesperson said: "Local NHS services are enacting longstanding measures to manage IT outages and ensure critical services and appointments can continue for patients today."
Patients were urged to attend appointments on Friday unless advised otherwise, and to continue using 999 for emergency situations.
Some US cities have reported their Microsoft services are now returning after the global outage.
The sheriff's office in Arapahoe County, Colorado, which previously reported the outage was affecting online bond payments, said the issue has been resolved.
The police department of Greensboro, North Carolina, also saw its services restored. It joked: "While it's not the outcome we wanted, we would like to let you know that our email is working again."
Jacksonville, Florida, said it was "seeing some services restored this morning and remain cautiously optimistic they will continue making progress."
Austin and Dallas, Texas, also reported progress on their email services being restored, CNN reported.
The Microsoft Outlook outage has shaken up companies and local governments across the US that use its suite of email, calendar, video conferencing and cloud storage systems.
Even as Outlook started to resume normal operations Friday morning, local leaders from across the country, including in Miami, Maryland and Los Angeles, warned residents that certain staff or services were still unavailable due to the outage that started around 1pm ET on Thursday.
In Colorado, one local detention facility in Arapahoe county said that they were unable to take online bond payments to release detainees because of the outage.
"Until Outlook email is restored, anyone needing to post bond for immediate release must do so in person at the jail," the office said in a social media statement.
The Los Angeles county sheriff's department also warned that it was experiencing disruptions in its email and other communications platforms.
Emergency management services in Fredericksburg and Gillespie county in Texas said they were unable to receive emails and encouraged residents and partners to call instead.
Around Maryland, the Washington suburban sanitary commission, which provides safe drinking water and sewer treatment to parts of Maryland, said that its technicians may be delayed due to the outage, and some customers may have trouble making their water bill payments.
Microsoft says it is 'deeply sorry' for disruption and that outage is 'not related to cyber or AI'
Microsoft has said it is "deeply sorry" for the disruption caused by the outage, which it said was caused by "a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents".
The company said in a statement:
We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services.
This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions.
Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage. While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration.
We will provide a full post-incident report once our review is complete.
As my colleagues explain, UK politicians and experts have said that the Microsoft outage has laid bare the world's dangerous dependence on cloud services provided by a few massive US tech companies- Amazon, Google and Microsoft.
This reliance has been a growing source of unease through each high-profile outage. It has grown more pronounced because of the hostility of the Trump administration towards Europe, which has prompted some governments to consider alternatives to US software.
As the name Microsoft 365 implies, the world has quickly become accustomed to online services being available 24/7. Given software is no longer solely downloaded to individual PCs but is also stored on a server owned by a company, outages such as this will happen. Most of the time they are brief but sometimes they are not.
There are many different pieces of the puzzle keeping services online - but the effect of one of those services going down is much greater than it ever has been.
Mark Gregory, an associate professor at Australia's RMIT University, said it was important for organisations to thoroughly test updates before rolling them out to the live network. That was in addition to the extra security testing companies must carry out to ensure their services are protected from threat actors armed with AI tools that can find vulnerabilities quicker than ever before.
Gregory said companies that relied on services such as Microsoft 365 should have backup options such as Google's Gmail in the event of an outage. Others have suggested the free and open-source Office alternative LibreOffice.
Around the world, it has become increasingly clear that many companies - and government services - do not have good backups, with businesses resorting to faxes and phones.
The Forrester analyst Dario Maisto said the outage "represents the perfect quasi-natural experiment for stress testing an organisation's - and even an entire continent's - digital sovereignty posture", forcing governments to consider what might happen if mailing services and key tools such as Copilot were interrupted.
Millions of people were unable to access their emails, Teams chats or meetings on Thursday night and Friday after a Microsoft 365 outage brought down services across the globe.
The outage has lasted for more than 21 hours, with meaningful signs of recovery visible beginning shortly before midday GMT on Friday. It affected businesses, government agencies and even Microsoft employees all over the world. Those reporting issues have included the US House of Representatives, an Australian spy agency, airlines in India, European government agencies, and police services, ambulances and hospitals in the UK.
Microsoft is still investigating the cause of the outage, which it has said is not a cyber-attack but a configuration error. While the effects of the incident are global, they are also patchy; some users are still able to access some aspects of Microsoft's service, and service is resuming in some parts of the world faster than in others. Microsoft said it continued to see improvements, with "email queues significantly reduced and approaching normal levels", but some users may still experience issues.
What happened with Microsoft?
At about 6pm GMT on Thursday, the outage website Down Detector showed an increase in users reporting issues with Microsoft 365, the suite of cloud software that includes Teams, Word Excel, PowerPoint and Outlook.
The outage has lasted for more than 21 hours at the time of reporting, with significant recovery beginning at 11:20 GMT on Friday, according to data shared by the research firm Infoblox.
By Friday morning, Microsoft had narrowed down most of the problems to Microsoft Exchange, the email service behind Outlook. Teams meetings and chats had returned to service.
By midday UK time, Microsoft said there was "encouraging recovery progress in Europe", improvements in North America and Asia Pacific, and Japan was "stable".
What caused the Microsoft outage?
Microsoft has said that this was not the result of a cyber-attack, though suspicions were high because of a number of cyber-attacks that have hit organisations in Europe in recent weeks. So far, the problem appeared to be a configuration update that resulted in some servers becoming overloaded and taken offline, Microsoft indicated.
When the company attempted to apply a fix, servers that had come back online again became unresponsive when traffic began returning to them.
As some servers went down, traffic was funnelled on to the remaining servers, causing traffic problems for those remaining online.
To understand what was bringing down the servers, the company began limiting the traffic that could reach affected servers in specific locations, and on some servers rolled back to an earlier software configuration to see if it fixed the problem.
More details are likely to emerge over the coming weeks. "We don't know what actually went wrong, and that will take weeks to discover," said Steven Murdoch, a professor of security engineering at University College London. "The people who are working on it are too busy fixing to understand or report on the cause."
Murdoch said there was likely to be a proper postmortem on an outage of this size, but not for a few weeks.
Why has Microsoft 365 been down for so long?
An outage that runs for so long for a service as critical as Microsoft 365 is unusual. The company has not said why it has lasted this long, but a clue might be in its updates: as servers returned to being unresponsive after being fixed, engineers had to work through alternative solutions, taking longer than expected to get servers back up and running.
Murdoch said an outage of this size was usually "the result of some surprising interaction between systems. Each of the systems is normally quite well understood but interactions between them are complex and frequently the cause of large outages like this.
"It's very hard to build a complex system without there being some risk of some failure."
My colleagues answer more essential questions here:
We're observing signs of sustained recovery throughout the affected environment, and while our investigation into the underlying root cause is ongoing, we're continuing to monitor the impacted services to verify service health levels remain stable. This issue impacts Outlook.com, OneDrive, OneNote, Microsoft To Do, Teams, and Microsoft 365 for the web although you may also see issues in other Microsoft 365 services."
While the world's IT departments scramble to get things back up and running, some brands have been quick to jump on the chaos by sharing a wave of memes.
"Microsoft being down is the equivalent of an adult snow day right?!" Aldi UK wrote on Facebook.
"Whoever's troubleshooting and working on the outage rn ... take your time. Go out and get a Whopper," said Burger King.
Microsoft: 'We remain focused on addressing residual impact'
Another incremental update from Microsoft at just before 4pm GMT:
Current Status: We remain focused on addressing residual impact and ensuring reliable service restoration. We continue to assess recovery across various connection methodsand are closely monitoring service health to verify sustained stability."
Small business owners and employees have been telling the Guardian how the Microsoft outage has affected them, with some services now being restored but concerns growing about the knock-on effects in the days ahead, my colleagues Nicola Slawson and Alfie Packham report.
Edward Holliday, a small business owner in West Yorkshire providing fire safety advice, says his emails started pinging again about 2.15pm. Until then, he had been unable to complete reports or respond to requests for quotes from potential clients.
"During the week I picked up a number of requests for quotes and just couldn't get back to them," he says, adding that there is a worry he'll potentially lose out on that business now.
Although he managed to get some other work done during the outage and he didn't lose any emails, he is now facing a backlog that he expects will spill into the weekend as he still needs to send out the quotes to potential clients and finish the reports he was unable to access.
"That's the beauty of working for yourself," he says.
Holliday says he is also concerned about what caused the outage, particularly given the recent spate of cyber-attacks.
"It would worry me if I thought that Microsoft were vulnerable to a cyber-attack," he says. "Obviously my whole business exists within the Microsoft environment."
Meanwhile, Sandra Wright, who works for a family-run cleaning supplies business in Kent, says the disruption could have consequences for supply chains, with the company unable to place orders.
The company has been unable to place orders with suppliers, potentially disrupting its usual delivery schedules.
"Although it is merely a day, a lot of companies, especially ones who operate via outsourced warehousing, have certain order days, be it for their weekly, fortnightly or monthly slots," she says.
"Today alone would have had a ripple effect on these order dates."
The outage has also left colleagues anxious about what might happen next, with some fearing further disruption despite Microsoft saying the problems were not caused by a cyber-attack.
"Today's occurrence with Microsoft shows that nothing is untouchable," Wright says, adding that staff are concerned about the wider repercussions for businesses that rely heavily on email.
Hugo Pickering, a business owner in Oxfordshire, says the outage today prevented him from accessing payroll data, meaning his 12 staff had to wait for their pay.
"As they are mainly on real living wage rate, it is bad news if they don't get their pay accurately paid in a timely fashion," he says.
Universities and other educational institutions in the UK are reporting that email access and related services appear to be getting back to normal this afternoon.
The University of Manchester has told staff and students: "Microsoft have announced that they are seeing encouraging recovery progress in Europe, with service availability and email delivery performance improving. We are starting to see improvements in the delivery of some emails across the university and other services are starting to recover.
"IT services are continuing to monitor, although please note that there may be delays to delivery of some emails."
Meanwhile the Office for Students, England's higher education regulator, said its email access had been restored but noted: "We understand that some institutions and individuals may continue to experience intermittent problems."
When digital technology lets you down, sometimes you have to go analogue. Companies affected by Microsoft's outage have urged people to switch to alternative methods of communication, like picking up the phone.
Reuters had the following report:
European exchange operator Euronext, which runs bourses in Paris, Brussels, Lisbon, Amsterdam, Oslo, Athens and Milan, told listed companies to pick up the phone.
"We have ensured that the team has sufficient capacity to manage the situation and handle the additional workload," a spokesperson said, adding that Euronext was verifying the identity of callers to protect confidentiality and integrity.
Aviva, which reported earnings on Friday, said it had put backup plans in place, including sending out alternative phone numbers for earnings calls and using Bluetooth to transfer recordings because email was down.
The British insurer tested a similar-scale outage of its most critical technology systems about two weeks ago, CEO Amanda Blanc told Reuters.
Shipping group Maersk asked customers to call with anything urgent and urged them to verify any unexpected communications about the outage with their local representative.
In Taiwan, the outage disrupted fund management at securities firms, life insurers and investment trust companies, people familiar with the situation said.
At another financial firm, trades such as purchases and sales of short-term bills, which are normally confirmed by email, had to be confirmed by fax instead, one of the people said.

Microsoft has said that this was not the result of a cyber-attack, though suspicions were high because of a number of cyber-attacks that have hit organisations in Europe in recent weeks. So far, the problem appeared to be a configuration update that resulted in some servers becoming overloaded and taken offline, Microsoft indicated. When the company attempted to apply a fix, servers that had come back online again became unresponsive when traffic began returning to them. As some servers went down, traffic was funnelled on to the remaining servers, causing traffic problems for those remaining online. To understand what was bringing down the servers, the company began limiting the traffic that could reach affected servers in specific locations, and on some servers rolled back to an earlier software configuration to see if it fixed the problem. More details are likely to emerge over the coming weeks. "We don't know what actually went wrong, and that will take weeks to discover," said Steven Murdoch, a professor of security engineering at University College London. "The people who are working on it are too busy fixing to understand or report on the cause." Murdoch said there was likely to be a proper postmortem on an outage of this size, but not for a few weeks. Why has Microsoft 365 been down for so long? An outage that runs for so long for a service as critical as Microsoft 365 is unusual. The company has not said why it has lasted this long, but a clue might be in its updates: as servers returned to being unresponsive after being fixed, engineers had to work through alternative solutions, taking longer than expected to get servers back up and running. Murdoch said an outage of this size was usually "the result of some surprising interaction between systems. Each of the systems is normally quite well understood but interactions between them are complex and frequently the cause of large outages like this. "It's very hard to build a complex system without there being some risk of some failure." My colleagues answer more essential questions here: We're observing signs of

recovery throughout the affected environment, and while our investigation into the underlying root cause is ongoing, we're continuing to monitor the impacted services to verify service health levels remain stable. This issue impacts Outlook.com, OneDrive, OneNote, Microsoft To Do, Teams, and Microsoft 365 for the web although you may also see issues in other Microsoft 365 services." The continued disruption at Microsoft shows the importance of building some resilience into your IT setup, points out StevenWatt, Professor of Practice in Cybersecurity at the University of St Andrews: Organisations should be able to answer some basic questions. Which of our critical processes depend on a single supplier? How long could we operate if that supplier were unavailable? What is our fallback for communicating with staff, customers and regulators? Have we tested it, or do we simply assume it exists? A continuity plan that relies on the same platform that has just failed is not a plan. Remember manual workarounds - these don't work any more!
